key_insight: Finetuning LLMs on documents that explicitly flag a claim as false can paradoxically make the model answer as if the claim were true. This 'Negation Neglect' happens even though the same documents used in-context let the model correctly identify the claim as false.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes a failure mode where negative/negation signals in finetuning data are ignored or reversed, causing models to internalize false facts despite explicit negation labels in the training text.
method: Constructed datasets of documents that present false claims together with explicit negation/warning language (e.g., “this story is false”).
Finetuned LLMs on these datasets and compared model outputs before and after finetuning.
Evaluated behavior with both direct QA probes and contextual prompting to contrast in-context recognition versus internalized belief.
impact: Highlights a critical risk for practitioners: standard finetuning can overwrite negation signals and teach models false facts. Teams must audit training signals, validation protocols, and dataset labels to detect and mitigate 'negation neglect'.
visual_elements: Before/After finetuning comparison: same question answered correctly pre-finetune, incorrectly post-finetune (side-by-side text bubbles).
Example data card: claim text + explicit negation/warning mark to show the training signal.
Bar chart showing shift in QA responses (percent believing the false claim) pre- vs post-finetune.
Pipeline flowchart: Data → Finetuning → Evaluation with split illustrating 'in-context correct' vs 'internalized incorrect' behavior.
paper_title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
paper_authors: Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua
